modelResponse.episodeSummary: 31-year-old male with acute pericarditis, presenting with sinus rhythm and stable hemodynamics.
keyECGEvidence: Diffuse concave (upward-scooping) ST elevation 1-2 mm in leads I, II, aVL, aVF, V3-V6
PR-segment depression in leads II, III, aVF, V4-V6
No reciprocal ST depression in any other lead
modelResponse.mechanism: Inflammation of the pericardium leading to subepicardial and epicardial irritation, manifesting as diffuse ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression.
contributingFactors: Recent Upper Respiratory Infection (URI) 1 week ago
Pleuritic chest pain (worse supine, improved leaning forward)
Pericardial friction rub heard on auscultation
Elevated CRP (4.8 mg/dL) and ESR (38 mm/hr)

rejectedAlternatives.why: ST elevation is diffuse and concave rather than localized; no reciprocal ST depression; patient is young with no cardiac risk factors; clinical presentation is pleuritic rather than pressure-like.

While the patient is young, the presence of a friction rub, elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 4.8 mg/dL), and acute onset of pleuritic pain strongly favors inflammatory pericarditis over benign early repolarization.

recommendedActions: Initiate NSAID therapy (e.g., Ibuprofen or Aspirin) as per clinical guidelines for pericarditis.
Provide supplemental oxygen if needed (though SpO2 is currently 99%).
Monitor for signs of cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad, pulsus paradoxus).
Serial troponin monitoring to rule out evolving myocardial involvement.
Continue monitoring of heart rate and blood pressure.
uncertainty: Troponin T is 'mild HIGH' (0.03 ng/mL), which can occur in pericarditis but requires monitoring to ensure it does not trend significantly higher.
WBC is 'mild HIGH' (11.2 10^3/uL), which is non-specific but consistent with recent URI/inflammation.
